results.title: Alloy Robotics Raises $11.5m at $115m Valuation | Joe Harris posted on the topic | LinkedIn
results.author: Joe Harris
highlights:
Today, we’re announcing another A$11.5m at a A$115m valuation 🤖 Bringing our total raised to over A$16m. The round was led by Square Peg, with continued support from Blackbird Airtree, Skip Capital and an incredible group of angels, founders and leaders from Tesla, Waymo, OpenAI, Anthropic and more. The investor support means a lot. But the signal that gave me the confidence to raise again came from our customers. A full day of robot test analysis now takes ten minutes. At Advanced Navigation, that has helped the validation team go from two tests per week to ten. Questions that once took weeks can now be answered the same day. Results like these are why Alloy Robotics has raised again, barely one year after we started. 🚀 Since launching publicly late last year, we have deployed Alloy across agriculture, defence, drones, medical devices, industrial systems, maritime robotics and humanoids. And we have learned something important: Robotics teams are not short of data. They are short on memory. The context needed to understand a robot is scattered across logs, images, tickets, code and the heads of individual engineers. When something fails, teams piece that context together manually. When it happens again six months later, much of the investigation starts from scratch. Alloy gives robotics teams and AI agents a shared memory over the data their machines produce. We understand the robot as a complete system across hardware, firmware and software, then bring answers into the tools where engineers already work. The principle is simple: - Every run should make the next one better. - Every test should improve the next design decision. - Every firmware update should carry the context of past fixes and regressions. - Every support ticket should draw on what the fleet has already experienced. That is the compounding loop we are building. This capital lets us move faster: expanding globally, deepening our robotics-specific intelligence and evaluation capabilities, and investing further in implementation and support. Our investment in service and partnership has been our unfair advantage, so we’re doubling down. I’m incredibly proud of the small, deeply technical and customer-obsessed team we have built. And I’m deeply grateful to our partners Jethro Cohen, Tom Humphrey, Jackie Vullinghs and Olivia Sioud (Grivas), our customers, and everyone who has backed us along the way. Raising capital is a means to an end. Helping teams build safer, better and more reliable machines is the goal. This is our life’s work: accelerating robotic intelligence and, ultimately, robotic abundance. If you’re building and deploying robots, I’d love to talk. If you want to help build this future, we’re hiring.
...

results.title: Alloy raises $4.5m to solve robotics data challenge | Joe Harris posted on the topic | LinkedIn
highlights:
It's official 🤖 I'm excited to announce Alloy, and our $4.5m pre-seed round led by Blackbird with support from Airtree, Xtal, Skip Capital and an incredible group of angels, leaders and founders of Tesla, Waymo, Carbon Robotics, Halter, Reach Robotics, Relevance AI and more. One of the strongest pre-seed rounds ever done in Australia and a testament to the calibre of the team and magnitude of the opportunity. At Alloy, we are building the system for robotics companies to reduce time spent on processing data by up to 90%, enabling 10x faster iteration. Instead of leaving behind 99% of their data in cold storage, teams can continuously improve performance. This is one of the most pressing problems in robotics: robotics teams are drowning in terabytes of data they can't efficiently search or analyze, forcing every company to build expensive custom infrastructure from scratch. And the problem only gets worse as you scale. When your robot encounters an issue, has it occurred before? How frequently? Will you know if it happens again? You’re often left with more questions than answers, and hundreds of hours of log files to scrub through. Companies like Waymo, Amazon and Tesla have deployed hundreds of engineers at this data infrastructure challenge. We are bringing best-in-class to the world. Alloy allows robotics teams to automatically organise, search & analyse across all types of multimodal robot data in one platform using natural language, without waiting for labels. Instantly summarise missions and share. Unprecedented levels of observability and data accessibility. We're currently working with pioneering robotics companies like Hullbot, Breaker and more, across oceanic inspections, defence AI, and maritime autonomy. Special thanks to Tom Humphrey at Blackbird, Jackie Vullinghs at Airtree, Fiona Leng at Xtal and Olivia Grivas at Skip Capital for believing in our vision and being great partners on this journey so far. This is just the beginning as we build the layer that is unlocking the next wave of scaled robotics companies. Day 1 at Alloy. More in comments.

snippets.title: Alloy Robotics Raises $11.5m at $115m Valuation | Joe Harris posted on the topic | LinkedIn
snippets.snippet: Today, we’re announcing another A$11.5m at a A$115m valuation 🤖 Bringing our total raised to over A$16m. The round was led by Square Peg, with continued support from Blackbird Airtree, Skip Capital and an incredible group of angels, founders and leaders from Tesla, Waymo, OpenAI, Anthropic and more. The investor support means a lot. But the signal that gave me the confidence to raise again came from our customers. A full day of robot test analysis now takes ten minutes. At Advanced Navigation, that has helped the validation team go from two tests per week to ten. Questions that once took weeks can now be answered the same day. Results like these are why Alloy Robotics has raised again, barely one year after we started. 🚀 Since launching publicly late last year, we have deployed Alloy across agriculture, defence, drones, medical devices, industrial systems, maritime robotics and humanoids. And we have learned something important: Robotics teams are not short of data. They are short on memory. The context needed to understand a robot is scattered across logs, images, tickets, code and the heads of individual engineers. When something fails, teams piece that context together manually.
